initiation.description: "user_asked": the user asked in words for separate, parallel or background work, or told you to start this piece — it starts now. "offer": a task the user named in their latest message (new work for this session, or one they asked you to suggest, split off or make a session for) — the user is asked first and the call waits for their answer; send only title with it (the brief follows, with proposal_id, if they choose New session). "own_initiative": work you propose yourself that the user has not told you to do — something you noticed, or the follow-up your own answer or work turned up; it waits as a proposal card until the user starts it; never for a task the user's message tells you to do. Required unless proposal_id is set.

proposal_id.description: Start a proposal the user told you to start, exactly as proposed: its task_id and nothing else (wake_when_done may accompany a local one). To change it, dismiss_task it and start a new session.

title.description: Under 60 chars; names the task. Shown on the row or card. Required unless proposal_id is set.

prompt.description: The brief: the task, the files or area, what done looks like. Required for "user_asked" and "own_initiative" — the call is refused without it, and `background` does not stand in for it; an "offer" leaves it out (the card shows the user's own message) and you send it with proposal_id once they choose New session.

context.description: "fresh" (default) or "fork" — see the tool description. A "fork" from a worktree session gets a fresh worktree, normally cut from your branch tip (commit first; uncommitted edits stay here); from a plain checkout it shares the folder.

background.description: Required with "fresh", besides `prompt`: at least 80 characters of overall goal, decisions and constraints so far, how this piece fits — for someone who has not seen this conversation. Ignored for "fork".

wake_when_done.description: Once this session (and any sibling still working) ends its turn, or fails to start (unless it waits at a prompt the user answers there, its folder was never opened in Claude Desktop, or the user started, stopped or archived it), and you are idle, the app continues you, whether or not this is set. true also continues you if this session never gets its task some other way, such as a brief that is not sent; default false; not with own_initiative; ignored with target "cloud", which never continues you.

name.description: Optional short handle for the session ([a-z0-9-], ≤24), e.g. "cli-cleanup". Linked sessions and plan steps refer to it by this name; derived from the title when omitted.

use_worktree.description: "fresh" only (rejected with "fork"). false = shares this session's checkout and can edit it (in a worktree session: its worktree, branch and PR, so never for work that ends in a branch or PR of its own or belongs in another repository); not accepted from a session set up to move from the user's checkout into a worktree with EnterWorktree (before or after it moves), one working in a worktree on an SSH host, or one whose worktree was given back. At another place named by `cwd`, `host` or `preset`, false = that folder as it is. true = its own git worktree. Omitted: the same folder when this session works in a plain folder and has never had a worktree (its own, a shared one, or one it will enter later); otherwise its own worktree. Omitted with `preset` or `host`, or with `cwd` from a session on an SSH host: the default set on that preset or SSH connection instead.

model.description: "fresh" only, optional: a cheaper model id for mechanical or read-only pieces (e.g. a Sonnet or Haiku id). Same family or cheaper than yours; anything higher is ignored. Omit to inherit yours.

target.description: "fresh" only. "local" (default) = where this session runs. "cloud" = run it as a cloud session (keeps going when this computer sleeps). Needs the repository on GitHub and a cloud environment — the app checks and tells the user if it cannot, and the task then stays as a card for them to start. It starts from this session's pushed branch when it runs in a worktree, else the repository's default branch. model/effort/use_worktree/cwd/source_branch do not apply. Only when the user asks for the cloud. "ssh" = on the SSH connection named by host (or by a preset).

host.description: With target "ssh": the name of one of the user's saved SSH connections (as list_start_targets reports it) — never a raw hostname, user or key. The app connects as the user configured it and may ask them to sign in.

cwd.description: The folder the session works in, when it is not this project: an absolute (or ~/) path on the host it will run on — this computer, this session's host, or the SSH connection named by host (default there: the connection's folder). Must exist; if the user has not trusted it yet the app asks them first. "fresh" only.

environment.description: With target "cloud": the name or id of one of the user's cloud environments (list_start_targets lists them); omitted = the default one. Self-hosted environments and runner pools need the user's own click and are refused, and so is an environment that cannot run this project's repository.

source_branch.description: The existing local branch the new worktree is cut from. Default in this project: this session's base branch (the one picked when it started, or the one its worktree was cut from). If the session has none and either it runs on an SSH host or its project folder is itself a git worktree or submodule, the folder's current commit. Otherwise, the repository's default branch, or the folder's current commit if that is unknown. Only for a session that gets its own worktree (use_worktree true, or the place's default); not with target "cloud".

branch_name.description: A short slug for the new worktree's branch (the app adds the user's branch prefix and a suffix). Only with a worktree.

preset.description: The name of one of the user's saved session presets on this computer: it names the place itself (a folder here or an SSH connection and folder — do not pass host or cwd with it) and brings model, effort and worktree defaults plus its saved environment variables; use_worktree/model/effort override those. Cloud and Remote Control presets are not available here.

effort.description: "fresh" only, optional: reasoning effort at or below yours. Omit to inherit.

permission_mode.description: Optional, local starts only: the permission mode it starts in — this session's own or a lower one (omit to inherit it). A higher mode, or one the app does not offer here, is refused; raising a session is set_session_permission_mode's card to show.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__update_plan
tools.description:
Keep the task list the app shows under your latest message while you work: the user follows your progress by it and will never ask for it, so it is part of the task. Every request that edits files or runs more than one command gets one (implement-and-test, investigate-then-fix, anything the user listed); only a single-command answer or pure conversation does not.

Never spend a message on this tool alone: send it IN THE SAME MESSAGE as another tool call (in parallel), so it costs no extra round trip.
- First call: with the VERY FIRST tool call of the turn, even one that only reads or lists files: {"items": [...]}, the whole plan in order, short imperative phrases (at most ~7 words, no numbering), the step you are starting "in_progress", the rest "pending". If you must look around first, make "Look at how X is set up" step one and refine the list once you know.
- Next step: {"advance": true} alongside the call that begins it (completes the in_progress step, starts the next pending one); after the last step, advance alongside wrap_up.
- Out of order: {"done": [2], "start": 4} (1-based).
- Plan changed, including right after the user interrupts or sends a new instruction mid-task: {"items": [...]} again, the new whole list, so the pinned list never shows an abandoned plan.
- Every {"items"} call says in "scope" what this request is to the session: "first_task" (nothing finished here yet); after that, "new_task" (unrelated work: it builds on nothing done, found or decided here) or "continuation" (everything else: anything a few tool calls settle, the next iteration, acting on what you just investigated or suggested, even if that work gets its own commit or PR; when unsure, this one). A "new_task" turn opens with a start_session offer and reaches this call only if the user chose Do it here.
Keep exactly one step in_progress while working and none when everything is done. Do not also write the plan as a numbered list in your message: the pinned list is the plan.

scope.description: Required with items: "first_task", "continuation" or "new_task" (see the tool description). Omit on advance / done / start updates.

content.description: The step, as a short imperative phrase (≤7 words).

session.description: When you delegated this step to a session you started: that session's short name (from start_session's result). The app shows its live state on the step.

items.description: The whole plan, in order (1–12 steps); replaces the previous list. Use on the first call and whenever the plan changes.

advance.description: true: the in_progress step is done and the next pending step starts (the cheap, usual update).

done.description: 1-based numbers of steps just completed (out-of-order updates).

start.description: 1-based number of the step now in progress (with done, for out-of-order updates).

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
tools.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: propose it and call this.

The result says which case below applies. When the box shows your question, it ends your turn: write no text after this call, since the recap and question say what the user needs and your work above holds the detail. Otherwise your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, with any question the box did not show.

Fields — recap and ask are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label and message are the user's words back to you:
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

recap.description: Two or three short sentences to the user (≤300 chars): what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified. Its first sentence is the sidebar status.

ask.description: The one question (≤100 chars) when the next move is the user's call — a choice, a go-ahead, an approval: the decision alone, with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give (actions[0] is your pick). Omit it, and actions, when nothing waits on the user.

blocked.description: true when your work stops here until the user answers (the app marks the session as waiting on them); omit when the answer can wait.

action.description: An app action update_plan's result listed as available now, or one your own work this turn made available; anything else is refused, and one that stops being available later is dropped (as actions[0], with your ask and the other answers), so do not guess. Omit for a reply.

label.description: For a reply: the button text, 1–3 words (4 only when three cannot say it) / 24 characters — "Yes, fix 1", "Fix 2 instead", "Not now": a button, not a sentence; the detail goes in message. No "@", no leading / or !. Ignored for an app action (the app's own label is used).

message.description: For a reply: what the click sends, up to 300 characters of plain text — no "@" anywhere, no leading / or !. Omit when the label is the whole message.

actions.description: 1–2 buttons, recommendation first. They are answers to your ask: the first accepts your recommendation, and another is there only when it is a realistic alternative the user might pick instead — not a menu of everything you mentioned. When blocked is true, they are the most likely answers to your question. While Auto-fix is on for the session's PR, none offers to watch it, fix CI, resolve conflicts or address comments.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
schema.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

name.description: Tool name (e.g. computer, navigate, find, form_input, read_page). browser_batch cannot be nested. A tabs_create's new tabId is only returned when the batch ends — load that tab in a later call.

input.description: That tool's input — same shape you'd pass when calling it directly. For computer items whose action is left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key or type, and for form_input items, include action_summary in the item's input, as you would when calling that tool directly.

actions.description: List of tool calls to execute sequentially. Example: [{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"left_click","ref":"ref_12"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"type","text":"hello"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"screenshot"}}]

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

query.description: Text to look for in an element's role, name or text (case-insensitive substring, e.g. "Sign in", "search", "Add to cart").

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Code_iOS_Simulator__control
tools.description: Run, test, and visually verify iOS apps in the iOS Simulator on this Mac. Use this whenever the user wants to see or try their iOS app — "run my app", "test this on iPhone", "does this look right?", "try the new screen" — not only when they mention the simulator by name. Simulator only: this tool cannot drive or stream a physical iPhone or iPad. If the user wants the app on their real device ("on my iPhone", "on my device"), build and deploy for the device with your normal build tools instead, and say the live panel only shows simulators. 'attach' opens a live panel so the user can watch — when the user wants to see the app, call 'attach' FIRST, before building: it is cheap, opens instantly on a booted simulator, and errors harmlessly when nothing is booted (boot or build, then retry it). 'launch' installs and launches a built .app — build it first, with the user's own build tooling or this server's 'build' tool when this session has it; launch re-attaches on its own, but do not rely on that instead of the early attach. Screenshots and tap/swipe/text verification are headless and need no panel. Don't open the panel when the user only asked to build/compile or to run unit tests. Coordinates are in device points (origin top-left); the 'launch' result reports the device's point dimensions.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Code_iOS_Simulator__control
schema.description: Run, test, and visually verify iOS apps in the iOS Simulator on this Mac. Use this whenever the user wants to see or try their iOS app — "run my app", "test this on iPhone", "does this look right?", "try the new screen" — not only when they mention the simulator by name. Simulator only: this tool cannot drive or stream a physical iPhone or iPad. If the user wants the app on their real device ("on my iPhone", "on my device"), build and deploy for the device with your normal build tools instead, and say the live panel only shows simulators. 'attach' opens a live panel so the user can watch — when the user wants to see the app, call 'attach' FIRST, before building: it is cheap, opens instantly on a booted simulator, and errors harmlessly when nothing is booted (boot or build, then retry it). 'launch' installs and launches a built .app — build it first, with the user's own build tooling or this server's 'build' tool when this session has it; launch re-attaches on its own, but do not rely on that instead of the early attach. Screenshots and tap/swipe/text verification are headless and need no panel. Don't open the panel when the user only asked to build/compile or to run unit tests. Coordinates are in device points (origin top-left); the 'launch' result reports the device's point dimensions.

action.description: What to do. 'attach' opens the live simulator panel for the user — call it BEFORE you build or launch, as soon as the user wants to see the app: on a booted simulator it opens immediately, and otherwise it returns a clear, harmless error (boot or build first, then retry it). Do not skip the early attach because 'launch' also attaches — the panel should be open before the build starts. The panel is the user's view, not a precondition — 'screenshot' and input actions work without it. Skip it only when the user has no interest in watching; 'launch' installs and launches an .app (it also re-attaches, but call 'attach' early rather than relying on that); 'screenshot' returns a PNG of the current screen; 'tap'/'swipe'/'text'/'button' inject input; 'touch_path' performs a single-finger drag along an arbitrary path (eased curves, long-press-then-drag); 'touch2_path' is the two-finger variant for pinch/rotate; 'open_url' opens a deep link; 'detach' closes the panel/stream. NOTE: a 'swipe' or 'touch_path' whose start point is on-screen and within 4pt of an edge performs the OS edge gesture instead of a plain drag — left=back, top=notification shade, bottom=home/app-switcher, right=Control Center (mapped to the current interface orientation). Start more than 4pt from the edge to drag or scroll content near the bezel.

app_path.description: For 'launch': path to the built .app bundle (e.g. DerivedData/.../Build/Products/Debug-iphonesimulator/MyApp.app).

device.description: Simulator name (e.g. 'iPhone 17 Pro') or UDID. Defaults to the simulator already attached, else the first booted one. The first use of a device asks the user for permission.

udid.description: Alias for 'device' (identical semantics: simulator name or UDID). Pass at most one of 'device' / 'udid'.

bundle_id.description: For 'launch': bundle identifier. If omitted, extracted from the .app's Info.plist.

points.description: For 'touch_path': touch path samples in device points. First point is touch-down; last is touch-up. dt_ms is the delay before that sample (0-1000, total clamped to 30s).

points2.description: For 'touch2_path': two-finger path samples in device points. Each sample carries both contacts (x1/y1, x2/y2); first is touch-down, last is touch-up. dt_ms is the delay before that sample (0-1000, total clamped to 30s).

duration.description: Seconds. For 'tap', >0.5 is a long-press. For 'swipe', the gesture duration (default 0.3).

url.description: For 'open_url': URL or scheme to open in the simulator.

Show visual content — SVG graphics, diagrams, charts, or interactive HTML widgets — that renders inline alongside your text response.
Use for flowcharts, architecture diagrams, dashboards, forms, calculators, data tables, games, illustrations, or any visual content.
The code is auto-detected: starts with <svg = SVG mode, otherwise HTML mode.
A global sendPrompt(text) function is available — it sends a message to chat as if the user typed it.
IMPORTANT: Call read_me before your first show_widget call. Do NOT narrate or mention the read_me call to the user — call it silently, then respond as if you went straight to building the visualization.

IMPORTANT: Call read_me before your first show_widget call. Do NOT narrate or mention the read_me call to the user — call it silently, then respond as if you went straight to building the visualization.

loading_messages.description: 1–4 loading messages shown to the user while the visual renders, each roughly 5 words long. Write them in the same language the user is using. Use 1 for simple visuals, more for complex ones. If the topic is serious — illness, disease, pandemics, death, grief, war, conflict, poverty, disaster, trauma, abuse, addiction, medical decisions, politically charged subjects, or anything where the reader might be personally affected — keep these BORING: describe what the code is doing in the dullest generic way, no jargon-as-drama, no evocative terms. Pandemic growth model — NOT ['Simulating patient zero', 'Modeling the curve'] (documentary-narrator voice), YES ['Setting up the model', 'Running the calculation']. Cancer timeline — NOT ['Charting the battle ahead'], YES ['Laying out the stages']. If you have to ask whether it's serious, it is. Otherwise, have fun — reach for alliteration, puns, personification, wordplay, whatever lands in that language. Playful examples — revenue chart: ['Bribing bars to stand taller', 'Asking Q4 where it went']; kanban: ['Herding cards into columns', 'Dragging, dropping, not stopping'].

title.description: Short snake_case identifier for this visual. Must be specific and disambiguating — if the conversation has multiple visuals, this title alone should tell you which one is being referenced (e.g. 'q4_revenue_by_product_line' not 'chart', 'oauth_login_flow' not 'diagram'). Also used as the download filename, so no spaces or special characters.

widget_code.description: SVG or HTML code to render. For SVG: raw SVG code starting with <svg> tag, must use CSS variables for colors. Example: <svg viewBox="0 0 700 400" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">...</svg>. For HTML: raw HTML content to render, do NOT include DOCTYPE, <html>, <head>, or <body> tags. Use CSS variables for theming. Keep background transparent and avoid top-level padding. Scripts are supported but execute after streaming completes.

content.content:
Exit code 1
# General Review Lessons

- Make a guard's zero-match check count only the matches it is meant to protect. Matches that are always present, like the guard's own allowed cases, keep the check from ever firing.
- Test a guard by planting a violation and by breaking its detection, and see it fail both times. A guard that passes on clean code proves nothing.
- Before acting on a review finding, check whether existing tests or contracts explain the current shape. A structural test can be why the code looks the way it does.
- When code reads a user-owned config into a typed struct and writes it back, keep the fields it does not model. Any new reason to rewrite the file otherwise silently deletes user data.
- Make a new outer timeout longer than every internal budget on that path. Otherwise the kill fires before the code's own graceful fallback.
- Before setting an explicit timeout, look up the platform's current default for that exact event; an explicit value can shorten the budget rather than add one.
- When splitting known from unknown JSON keys to preserve them, decode only the exact known keys and keep every other key, case variants included, as unknown. `encoding/json` matches field names case-insensitively, so decoding the whole object lets a key like `"Command"` overwrite the real field.
- When a change makes a fix command riskier, changes which command to run, or adds a new place that reports an existing failure, check every place that already reports it (status, doctor, enable, help text) so they all give the same fix. Otherwise one screen sends people to the safe fix and the next to the destructive one, or one command prints the same failure twice with different fixes.
- When a test plants a failure to cover an error branch, make sure an earlier step doesn't fail first; otherwise the assertion passes without ever running that branch.
- Select an agent's final report by a marker it carries (such as the contract line), not by its position in the event stream; a trailing tool call or an empty message ID moves a position-based boundary.
- When code keeps state so a later run can retry, test the retry itself. A test that checks the kept state against the same expression the code uses would pass even if that expression were wrong.
- When decoding user-editable JSON into maps or pointers, skip null elements before writing to them; `[null]` decodes to a nil map and a write panics.
- Review a PR that is behind main against current main, not its own base: build both and run the same repro. Its tests pass on its old base even when keeping its side of a conflict would undo a fix merged since.
- When wiring user config into a new path, test it with a broken config too. A user rule that silently fails to load leaks the same way as one that was never wired.
- Make a fail-closed check fire only on the failure it guards against, not on a whole class of errors. A refusal on any settings error blocks unrelated cases and pushes users toward a less safe escape hatch, such as an unredacted `--raw` bundle.

# General Review Lessons

- Make a guard's zero-match check count only the matches it is meant to protect. Matches that are always present, like the guard's own allowed cases, keep the check from ever firing.
- Test a guard by planting a violation and by breaking its detection, and see it fail both times. A guard that passes on clean code proves nothing.
- Before acting on a review finding, check whether existing tests or contracts explain the current shape. A structural test can be why the code looks the way it does.
- When code reads a user-owned config into a typed struct and writes it back, keep the fields it does not model. Any new reason to rewrite the file otherwise silently deletes user data.
- Make a new outer timeout longer than every internal budget on that path. Otherwise the kill fires before the code's own graceful fallback.
- Before setting an explicit timeout, look up the platform's current default for that exact event; an explicit value can shorten the budget rather than add one.
- When splitting known from unknown JSON keys to preserve them, decode only the exact known keys and keep every other key, case variants included, as unknown. `encoding/json` matches field names case-insensitively, so decoding the whole object lets a key like `"Command"` overwrite the real field.
- When a change makes a fix command riskier, changes which command to run, or adds a new place that reports an existing failure, check every place that already reports it (status, doctor, enable, help text) so they all give the same fix. Otherwise one screen sends people to the safe fix and the next to the destructive one, or one command prints the same failure twice with different fixes.
- When a test plants a failure to cover an error branch, make sure an earlier step doesn't fail first; otherwise the assertion passes without ever running that branch.
- Select an agent's final report by a marker it carries (such as the contract line), not by its position in the event stream; a trailing tool call or an empty message ID moves a position-based boundary.
- When code keeps state so a later run can retry, test the retry itself. A test that checks the kept state against the same expression the code uses would pass even if that expression were wrong.
- When decoding user-editable JSON into maps or pointers, skip null elements before writing to them; `[null]` decodes to a nil map and a write panics.
- Review a PR that is behind main against current main, not its own base: build both and run the same repro. Its tests pass on its old base even when keeping its side of a conflict would undo a fix merged since.

date: August 24, 2026

### process_sessions condensation: step-by-step mental model

`PostCommit` condensation connects evolving Entire sessions to a Git commit durable checkpoint. Its current one-session-at-a-time storage model causes superlinear latency; safe batching must preserve ordering, attribution, routing, recovery, and cleanup invariants.

1. Entire session versus Git commit. An Entire session records an agent conversation, transcript, files touched, token usage, and temporary work. A Git commit records saved code changes. The post-commit hook connects relevant sessions to the new Git commit.

2. Temporary session data versus permanent checkpoint. While an agent works, session data continues evolving and may be stored in session state and shadow Git refs. Condensation converts this temporary representation into durable checkpoint data.

3. One commit can contain multiple sessions. A Git commit receives one `Entire-Checkpoint` ID, but its checkpoint can contain sessions A, B, C, and others. Twenty relevant sessions therefore mean one checkpoint ID containing twenty session entries.

4. Current storage is one session at a time. For twenty sessions sharing one checkpoint, `PostCommit` performs twenty separate session-storage writes.

5. Each write rebuilds and republishes the checkpoint. Writing A publishes `{A}`. Writing B loads `{A}`, reconstructs it, adds B, and publishes `{A,B}`. Writing C reconstructs `{A,B}`, adds C, and publishes `{A,B,C}`.

6. Repeated rebuilding creates triangular work. Three sessions require approximately `1 + 2 + 3 = 6` session-units instead of 3. Four require `1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10`. In general, the growing work resembles `N(N+1)/2`.

7. The measurements confirm superlinear behavior. Condensations grew from 67 to 335, a 5x increase, while storage grew from 1.185s to 23.243s, a 19.6x increase.

8. Storage is the smoking gun. Non-storage work stayed near 36-39ms per condensation, while storage rose from 17.7ms to 69.4ms. `find_sessions_for_worktree` remained only 17-74ms.

9. Batching changes the publication boundary. Entire should prepare A, B, and C separately, then build `{A,B,C}`, create one Git commit, and move the checkpoint ref once. Necessary transcript and attribution work remains per session.

10. A naive batch is unsafe. Storage could successfully contain B while saving B local state fails. Retrying by appending would duplicate B.

11. Retries must reuse the checkpoint ID and upsert by `SessionID`. If B already exists in Checkpoint X, retry replaces or updates B slot instead of appending another B.

12. Generation checks protect concurrent work. If B was prepared at generation 5 but advances to generation 6 before finalization, Entire must not overwrite generation 6 with stale state.

13. A published older snapshot remains valid. Checkpoint X may retain B valid generation-5 snapshot while B newer generation-6 state and shadow data remain available for a later checkpoint.

14. Checkpoint recovery completes interrupted condensation. A crash may occur after checkpoint publication but before state saving or cleanup. Recovery determines whether the session already exists, finishes its state transition when safe, or retries the same checkpoint ID.

15. Cleanup must happen last. A session shadow ref and completed task records remain until durable checkpoint storage and that session state save both succeed. Preparation in memory is not durable.

16. Cleanup success is per session. After a batch publication, A may finalize successfully while B remains pending. A can become cleanup-eligible, while B recovery data remains protected.

17. Routing is decided once per checkpoint. All sibling sessions sharing Checkpoint X must use the same `git-branch` or `git-refs` backend. Routing each session independently could split one logical checkpoint across backends.

18. Mirrors receive the complete batch. The batch must remain intact through routing, primary publication, and mirror fanout. Otherwise mirrors would continue rebuilding `{A}`, `{A,B}`, and `{A,B,C}` separately.

19. Combined attribution cannot sum individual percentages. Multiple sessions can observe the same changed file, so adding their independent attribution would double-count lines.

20. Combined attribution uses the finalized trustworthy set. Entire takes the union of files from successfully prepared sessions with trustworthy `SaveStepCount` data, diffs the Git commit once, and classifies changed files as agent or human.

21. Existing sessions under the same checkpoint participate. If Checkpoint X already contains A and a retry adds C, combined attribution must be recalculated over the final set `{A,C}`, not C alone. Sessions under another checkpoint do not participate.

22. Preserve post-write semantics without requiring post-publication. Assemble the complete candidate tree in memory, inspect its finalized session metadata, calculate combined attribution, add it to the candidate, and then publish once.

23. Attribution remains fail-soft. Failure to calculate derived attribution must not discard durable session data. Sessions can still be published without combined attribution, with the failure recorded for diagnosis or backfill.

24. A smaller per-write optimization is incomplete. Faster aggregation or tree surgery would still create hundreds of intermediate Git commits and ref updates. Batching aligns storage with the natural operation: one checkpoint from one Git commit.

25. Safe batching begins with ordered selection. Sessions are evaluated in stable order. Already-complete sessions are skipped. A session with an interrupted older checkpoint ID is preserved for recovery under that old ID rather than moved into the new checkpoint.

26. Preparation does not claim success. Each eligible session produces an immutable payload containing transcript, prompts, files, tasks, tokens, attribution, and expected generation. No state or recovery data is cleaned yet.

27. Assembly performs ordered upserts. The storage layer loads the checkpoint once, combines existing entries with prepared payloads, upserts by `SessionID`, aggregates once, and builds one complete candidate.

28. Publication is the batch-wide durability boundary. One Git tree, commit, and ref update makes the candidate durable. If primary publication fails, no session may be marked condensed.

29. Finalization remains per session. Each state is reloaded, its generation checked, and its checkpoint baselines saved. Only successfully finalized sessions become cleanup-eligible.

30. A durable journal makes the operation resumable. The journal records the checkpoint ID, stable session order, expected generations, publication state, and each session outcome.

31. Journal entries have safe outcomes. `Finalized` means state saved and cleanup allowed. `Superseded` means newer work exists and must be preserved. `Pending` means recovery must retry and cleanup remains forbidden. The journal completes only when no entry is pending.

32. The performance test must exercise real condensation. Hundreds of already-condensed session files only test scanning. The corrected fixture uses full history, unique bases and shadow trees, packed refs, real transcripts, committed-file overlap, and a realistic phase mix.

33. Cold runs prevent misleading cache wins. Cold measurements ensure Git objects, `packed-refs`, and filesystem metadata are not already cached and shared synthetic objects do not hide the growing-tree cost.

34. Final recommendation. Batch one checkpoint ID in stable session order, assemble attribution from the finalized candidate, publish one complete tree per backend, retry through idempotent `SessionID` upserts, and protect state transitions with a durable journal and generation checks.

Sources: `GitHub issue #2091`, `docs/architecture/commit-hook-perf-analysis.md`, `cmd/entire/cli/strategy/manual_commit_hooks.go`, `cmd/entire/cli/strategy/manual_commit_condensation.go`, `cmd/entire/cli/strategy/session_state.go`, `cmd/entire/cli/checkpoint/persistent.go`, `cmd/entire/cli/checkpoint/refs_store.go`, `cmd/entire/cli/checkpoint/routing_store.go`, `cmd/entire/cli/checkpoint/fanout.go`, `cmd/entire/cli/strategy/commit_hook_perf_test.go`.

### process_sessions condensation: step-by-step mental model

`PostCommit` condensation connects evolving Entire sessions to a Git commit durable checkpoint. Its current one-session-at-a-time storage model causes superlinear latency; safe batching must preserve ordering, attribution, routing, recovery, and cleanup invariants.

1. Entire session versus Git commit. An Entire session records an agent conversation, transcript, files touched, token usage, and temporary work. A Git commit records saved code changes. The post-commit hook connects relevant sessions to the new Git commit.

2. Temporary session data versus permanent checkpoint. While an agent works, session data continues evolving and may be stored in session state and shadow Git refs. Condensation converts this temporary representation into durable checkpoint data.

3. One commit can contain multiple sessions. A Git commit receives one `Entire-Checkpoint` ID, but its checkpoint can contain sessions A, B, C, and others. Twenty relevant sessions therefore mean one checkpoint ID containing twenty session entries.

4. Current storage is one session at a time. For twenty sessions sharing one checkpoint, `PostCommit` performs twenty separate session-storage writes.

5. Each write rebuilds and republishes the checkpoint. Writing A publishes `{A}`. Writing B loads `{A}`, reconstructs it, adds B, and publishes `{A,B}`. Writing C reconstructs `{A,B}`, adds C, and publishes `{A,B,C}`.

6. Repeated rebuilding creates triangular work. Three sessions require approximately `1 + 2 + 3 = 6` session-units instead of 3. Four require `1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10`. In general, the growing work resembles `N(N+1)/2`.

7. The measurements confirm superlinear behavior. Condensations grew from 67 to 335, a 5x increase, while storage grew from 1.185s to 23.243s, a 19.6x increase.

8. Storage is the smoking gun. Non-storage work stayed near 36-39ms per condensation, while storage rose from 17.7ms to 69.4ms. `find_sessions_for_worktree` remained only 17-74ms.

9. Batching changes the publication boundary. Entire should prepare A, B, and C separately, then build `{A,B,C}`, create one Git commit, and move the checkpoint ref once. Necessary transcript and attribution work remains per session.

10. A naive batch is unsafe. Storage could successfully contain B while saving B local state fails. Retrying by appending would duplicate B.

11. Retries must reuse the checkpoint ID and upsert by `SessionID`. If B already exists in Checkpoint X, retry replaces or updates B slot instead of appending another B.

12. Generation checks protect concurrent work. If B was prepared at generation 5 but advances to generation 6 before finalization, Entire must not overwrite generation 6 with stale state.

13. A published older snapshot remains valid. Checkpoint X may retain B valid generation-5 snapshot while B newer generation-6 state and shadow data remain available for a later checkpoint.

14. Checkpoint recovery completes interrupted condensation. A crash may occur after checkpoint publication but before state saving or cleanup. Recovery determines whether the session already exists, finishes its state transition when safe, or retries the same checkpoint ID.

15. Cleanup must happen last. A session shadow ref and completed task records remain until durable checkpoint storage and that session state save both succeed. Preparation in memory is not durable.

16. Cleanup success is per session. After a batch publication, A may finalize successfully while B remains pending. A can become cleanup-eligible, while B recovery data remains protected.

17. Routing is decided once per checkpoint. All sibling sessions sharing Checkpoint X must use the same `git-branch` or `git-refs` backend. Routing each session independently could split one logical checkpoint across backends.

18. Mirrors receive the complete batch. The batch must remain intact through routing, primary publication, and mirror fanout. Otherwise mirrors would continue rebuilding `{A}`, `{A,B}`, and `{A,B,C}` separately.

19. Combined attribution cannot sum individual percentages. Multiple sessions can observe the same changed file, so adding their independent attribution would double-count lines.

20. Combined attribution uses the finalized trustworthy set. Entire takes the union of files from successfully prepared sessions with trustworthy `SaveStepCount` data, diffs the Git commit once, and classifies changed files as agent or human.

21. Existing sessions under the same checkpoint participate. If Checkpoint X already contains A and a retry adds C, combined attribution must be recalculated over the final set `{A,C}`, not C alone. Sessions under another checkpoint do not participate.

22. Preserve post-write semantics without requiring post-publication. Assemble the complete candidate tree in memory, inspect its finalized session metadata, calculate combined attribution, add it to the candidate, and then publish once.

23. Attribution remains fail-soft. Failure to calculate derived attribution must not discard durable session data. Sessions can still be published without combined attribution, with the failure recorded for diagnosis or backfill.

24. A smaller per-write optimization is incomplete. Faster aggregation or tree surgery would still create hundreds of intermediate Git commits and ref updates. Batching aligns storage with the natural operation: one checkpoint from one Git commit.

25. Safe batching begins with ordered selection. Sessions are evaluated in stable order. Already-complete sessions are skipped. A session with an interrupted older checkpoint ID is preserved for recovery under that old ID rather than moved into the new checkpoint.

26. Preparation does not claim success. Each eligible session produces an immutable payload containing transcript, prompts, files, tasks, tokens, attribution, and expected generation. No state or recovery data is cleaned yet.

27. Assembly performs ordered upserts. The storage layer loads the checkpoint once, combines existing entries with prepared payloads, upserts by `SessionID`, aggregates once, and builds one complete candidate.

28. Publication is the batch-wide durability boundary. One Git tree, commit, and ref update makes the candidate durable. If primary publication fails, no session may be marked condensed.

29. Finalization remains per session. Each state is reloaded, its generation checked, and its checkpoint baselines saved. Only successfully finalized sessions become cleanup-eligible.

30. A durable journal makes the operation resumable. The journal records the checkpoint ID, stable session order, expected generations, publication state, and each session outcome.

31. Journal entries have safe outcomes. `Finalized` means state saved and cleanup allowed. `Superseded` means newer work exists and must be preserved. `Pending` means recovery must retry and cleanup remains forbidden. The journal completes only when no entry is pending.

32. The performance test must exercise real condensation. Hundreds of already-condensed session files only test scanning. The corrected fixture uses full history, unique bases and shadow trees, packed refs, real transcripts, committed-file overlap, and a realistic phase mix.

33. Cold runs prevent misleading cache wins. Cold measurements ensure Git objects, `packed-refs`, and filesystem metadata are not already cached and shared synthetic objects do not hide the growing-tree cost.

34. Final recommendation. Batch one checkpoint ID in stable session order, assemble attribution from the finalized candidate, publish one complete tree per backend, retry through idempotent `SessionID` upserts, and protect state transitions with a durable journal and generation checks.

created: 2026-08-26T07:07:48Z updated: 2026-09-01T06:43:57Z author: MuskanPaliwal
labels: 
reviewRequests: cli-maintainers

## Problem

`process_sessions` still persists each session separately. For every session, it reloads the checkpoint, rebuilds the session index and summary, creates a commit, and advances the checkpoint ref.

Issue #2091 measures that work at roughly 73–103 ms per session. The repeated checkpoint load and rebuild make condensation slower as more sessions share a checkpoint.

Checkpoint-level batching needs two things first:

- Ref updates must detect concurrent writes from hooks, worktrees, CLI processes, and other Git clients.
- Both persistent Git layouts must use the same batch algorithm.

## Solution

This PR adds native compare-and-swap publication and a shared `BatchSessions` write request.

It lays the storage and concurrency groundwork for #2091 item 2. It does not yet change PostCommit to group and submit sessions in batches. That work is listed below.

## Native compare-and-swap publication

`CompareAndSwapRef` publishes refs through native Git:

```text
git update-ref <ref> <new> <expected-old>
```

Missing-ref creation passes the correct all-zero object ID in both SHA-1 and SHA-256 repositories.

`RunRefTransaction` retries a logical mutation when another writer wins the race. Each attempt reads the current tip, rebuilds from that tip, and publishes with CAS. Conflicts use bounded, cancellation-aware jitter. The transaction stops after 16 attempts.

A mutation that reports `changed=false` is an idempotent no-op and does not call `git update-ref`.

The CAS conversion covers persistent v1 metadata refs and per-checkpoint refs, including:

- initial ref creation;
- v1 migration;
- attribution, summary, and transcript backfills;
- reconciliation and safe local ref advancement;
- orphan cleanup and expected-old deletion;
- shadow-branch migration;
- rewind publication;
- OPF publication.

OPF uses one CAS attempt by design. If its expected ref has moved, it fails closed and withholds the push. It does not rebuild sanitized output from newly appeared content.

Go-git object construction now takes a process-local lock keyed by `*git.Repository`. This protects go-git state shared by concurrent writers in one process. Native Git CAS handles publication conflicts between processes.

## Checkpoint-level batch writes

`BatchSessions` is now part of the sealed `WriteRequest` union. One request contains a checkpoint ID and one or more reserved session writes.

Validation happens before object construction:

- The checkpoint ID must be present and valid.
- Every session must reference that checkpoint.
- Session IDs must be valid and unique.
- Sessions are sorted by `SessionID`.
- Task tool-use IDs and agent IDs must be valid.
- Duplicate task IDs within or across incoming sessions are rejected.
- Sessions without timestamps share one UTC timestamp, truncated to seconds.
- Author fallback, commit-message inputs, and prepared tree hashes are fixed before CAS retries.

`GitStore` and `gitRefsStore` share the same preparation and checkpoint-tree builder. Their wrappers only locate or splice the checkpoint subtree and choose the ref to publish.

For each CAS attempt, the builder:

- loads the existing checkpoint once;
- reads each existing session’s metadata once;
- reuses the numeric index when updating a session;
- preserves untouched session subtree hashes;
- appends new sessions in canonical order;
- merges the task subtree once and preserves untouched tasks;
- reduces the complete final session set into the root summary;
- preserves combined attribution and sticky review, investigation, and import flags;
- aggregates counts, tokens, files, strategy, branch, and commit SHA deterministically;
- creates one checkpoint commit for that backend attempt.

Existing `Session` and `ReservedSession` requests pass through the same builder with one session. Their caller contract does not change.

Combined attribution stays in its existing backfill transaction. The batch write does not fold it into the checkpoint commit.

## Storage and compatibility

The durable checkpoint format does not change:

```text
metadata.json
0/metadata.json
0/full.jsonl
0/transcript.jsonl
1/...
tasks/<tool-use-id>/...
```

Older clients already understand checkpoints with multiple numbered session directories. A batch produces the same tree, task subtree, summary, and metadata types that repeated single-session writes produce.

Compatibility was checked in separate dimensions:

- New clients continue to read existing checkpoint data.
- Old clients can read checkpoints written by `BatchSessions`.
- Existing callers still use `Writer.Write(context.Context, WriteRequest)`.
- Single-session requests keep their existing behavior.
- Malformed or ambiguous requests now fail before publication.
- Concurrent upgraded writers protect each other with native CAS.
- If an old blind writer publishes first, the CAS writer detects the change and rebuilds.
- If an old blind writer publishes second, it can still overwrite the newer write. One upgraded participant cannot make a pre-CAS writer safe.

Rejecting invalid input and replacing last-writer-wins behavior with conflict detection are intentional safety changes, not storage incompatibilities.

## Routing and partial success

Persistent dispatch, kind routing, fanout, and the filesystem test store support `BatchSessions`.

One Git backend makes every session in the batch visible through one ref update. Fanout writes the primary first. Mirror failures remain logged and best-effort, so they do not turn a successful primary write into an error.

Routing follows the backend encoded by the checkpoint ID if configuration changes after reservation. If a readable migrated copy exists, routing updates that copy too. The read-preferred backend is probed before the first physical write.

There is no transaction across physical backends. If the second backend fails, the first may already contain the batch. The writer returns the error. Retrying the same canonical upsert repairs the lagging copy.

A future lifecycle caller must therefore treat an error as “some backend may already contain this batch,” not as proof that nothing was written.

The filesystem store replaces one JSON document atomically under a process-local mutex. It is a test backend and does not provide cross-process serialization.

## Complexity

The deterministic visitation test uses existing checkpoints with 100, 200, and 500 sessions. With no tasks, it records:

```text
root entries visited          N + 1
session entries visited       N
existing metadata reads       N
task entries visited          0
```

`CompareAndSwapRef` publishes refs through native Git:

- shadow-branch migration;
- rewind publication;
- OPF publication.

content.content:
Hey @Soph , Thanks for flagging this. Before I resolve the overlap, this is the shape I’m planning.

#2131 already has the first two parts of the batching work:

- A shared ref transaction API that reads the current tip, rebuilds against it, and publishes with native Git CAS.
- A `BatchSessions` storage request and shared builder for both `git-branch` and `git-refs`.

The storage-level batching is implemented. It can load one checkpoint, upsert several sessions, recompute the summary once, build one commit, and publish it once. Single-session writes also use that builder.

What #2131 does not do yet is use `BatchSessions` from `PostCommit`. The `process_sessions` loop still calls `CondenseSession` once per session, and each call writes one `ReservedSession`. That lifecycle change is planned for Stage 3.

The direct overlap with #1926 is the persistent-ref transaction code. Both PRs implement native CAS, retry, and rebuild behavior around many of the same writers. #1926 also adds some behavior that #2131 currently lacks:

- A cross-process filesystem lock for each persistent ref.
- Context-aware waiting for the lock.
- Holding the lock across the full read, build, CAS, and retry cycle.
- Cleaning up a losing commit only after a confirmed CAS conflict.
- The concurrent two-Stop-hook integration regression.

My plan is to keep #2131’s transaction API rather than carry `persistent_ref_update.go` forward as a second implementation. I would move #1926’s guarantees into `RunRefTransaction` and the multi-ref transaction path.

The result should work like this:

- The transaction acquires #1926’s per-ref filesystem lock before reading the tip.
- It holds the lock while building and publishing the commit.
- Native Git CAS remains the final publication check.
- If an external writer bypasses Entire’s lock and moves the ref, the transaction rereads the winning tip and rebuilds.
- Multi-ref transactions acquire all required ref locks in a fixed order before using the atomic multi-ref CAS path.
- Losing commits are removed only after confirmed CAS conflicts. Hard errors preserve them because Git may already have published the ref.

The process-local mutex in #2131 and the filesystem lock from #1926 have different jobs. The mutex protects go-git object construction from goroutines in one CLI process. The filesystem lock coordinates separate Entire processes. Git CAS protects the final ref update, including against tools that do not use Entire’s lock.

I would also keep the intent of #1926’s tests. Cooperating Entire writers should serialize on the filesystem lock. A simulated external Git writer should bypass the lock and exercise the CAS retry path. The concurrent Stop-hook integration regression should remain as end-to-end coverage.

Stage 3 would keep this locking. It would group prepared sessions by checkpoint ID and submit one `BatchSessions` write, so the persistent-ref lock is acquired once for the checkpoint batch instead of once per session. The remaining Stage 3 work is in the lifecycle: preparing sessions without immediately writing them, durable recovery intent, state finalization after publication, partial-backend retries, attribution, telemetry, and safe shadow-branch cleanup.

So the merge rule I’m proposing is: keep #2131’s transaction and batching structure, but carry #1926’s locking, cleanup, cancellation, and concurrency guarantees into that structure.

--- b126c2e8f stat:
b126c2e8f Record turn-end work in session state instead of a shadow branch
Every agent turn used to commit a full tree snapshot (code plus a redacted
copy of the metadata directory) to a per-base, per-worktree shadow branch
entire/<commit>-<worktree>. That is where the storage growth came from,
and the branch was the source of truth for everything downstream: commit
linking, carry-forward, condensation, lifecycle gates, pending rows and
explain. Deleting it at the wrong moment (pre-push and post-condense
cleanup) made uncondensed work unreachable.

Turn end now writes no git objects. SaveStep records the step in session
state: StepCount, FilesTouched, and TouchedFileHashes, the blob hash of
each touched regular file as the agent left it, computed with git
hash-object so clean filters apply as `git add` would ("" marks a
recorded deletion; an absent entry falls back to name matching). Hashing
runs outside the session lock, and a step path that is neither present
nor a recorded deletion is dropped as a transcript-parsing phantom. The
sanitized transcript copy under .entire/metadata/<session>/ stays as
before and is what condensation reads when the live transcript is gone.

Consumers move onto that state:

  - Commit linking compares the committed or staged blob of a new file
    with its recorded hash; the hunk-level comparison is gone.
  - Carry-forward keeps a path while its recorded content is not what
    was committed and the worktree still differs; remaining files stay
    in state (StepCount=1, transcript offsets reset) instead of being
    rewritten onto a new shadow commit.
  - Lifecycle gates (condense-by-ID, eager and session-end condensation,
    orphan deletion, the zombie sweep, doctor) ask State.HasPendingWork
    instead of whether a shadow ref exists. HasPendingWork ignores
    FullyCondensed; the sweep, IsCondensableEndedSession and doctor's
    ENDED classification still exclude fully condensed sessions, so a
    dead session is not re-condensed into IDLE on every commit.
  - BaseCommit simply follows HEAD (syncBaseCommitToHead, rewrite
    remapping); there is no branch to migrate.
  - Task-record completion, per-tool hooks and Codex child-file merges
    add paths through MergeUnhashedFilesTouched, which drops any older
    recorded hash so a rewritten file is not judged against it.

Removed with the writer: the ephemeral store and shadow ref locking,

# Checkpoint-Level Batching for `process_sessions` Condensation

Status: Stages 1 and 2 are implemented in the working tree; Stage 3 remains a
design. Tracks entireio/cli#2091 item 2.

This document was independently re-audited against `upstream/main` at
`e65edd125db622ece151578fb6ba68368831226b` on 2026-08-25. The design chooses
deterministic multi-session locking and idempotent republish recovery. A small
durable batch-membership intent closes the crash gap between separate session
reservation saves; it is not a snapshot generation. The design does not use
the checkpoint ID as a state generation and does not leave a lock-free build
protocol as an alternative implementation.

## 1. Problem and direction

`PostCommit` currently condenses each eligible session into the commit's shared
checkpoint one at a time (`manual_commit_hooks.go`, the `process_sessions`
loop). Every successful session reaches `store.Write(ReservedSession)`. Both
persistent backends then read the checkpoint's existing subtree, flatten it,
replace one session, recompute the checkpoint summary, rebuild a tree, create a
commit, and advance a persistent ref.

For N sessions accumulated under one checkpoint, the i-th sequential write
processes O(i) existing checkpoint data. The total is therefore
`1 + 2 + ... + N = O(N^2)`. Issue #2091 and the hook-performance analysis both
identify this as the largest remaining non-network opportunity in PostCommit.

Checkpoint-level batching remains the right direction:

- keep a `BatchSessions` persistent write request;
- keep one backing-independent batch tree builder shared by git-branch and
  git-refs;
- hold all relevant session locks across snapshot, build, ref transaction, and
  state updates;
- durably record the intended batch membership before publication, then recover
  interrupted work by idempotently upserting current locked state into the same
  checkpoint ID;
- publish through a generic native-Git CAS transaction used by every writer of
  the relevant persistent refs; and
- make checkpoint-content visitation linear by isolating work to individual

entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

When an event lands that the user would want to act on now — an error appeared, the status they were waiting on flipped — send a PushNotification. Not every event is worth a push; the ones that change what they'd do next are.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.
